headline: UNILEVER SAYS IT NOW HAS 500,000 PEOPLE MAKING CONTENT FOR IT, UP FROM 20,000 TWO YEARS AGO, AND ITS CHIEF EXECUTIVE TOLD INVESTORS THAT AFTER FOUR DAYS A VIDEO DOES NOT JUST STOP WORKING, IT STARTS LOSING MONEY
deck: One of the largest advertisers on earth has put a shelf life on video, out loud, in a published transcript.  Four days.  After that Fernando Fernandez says the return is not smaller, it is negative.  Read that number against how long your own videos take to make and something uncomfortable falls out.
tldr: Unilever's chief executive told investors that a video's lifespan is now four days and that after four days the return is negative rather than merely diminishing, while the company has gone from 20,000 to 500,000 people making content for it in two years and says the engagement its content earns, not the size of its media buy, now sets the price it pays.  Plot your last four campaigns day by day for three weeks, find where each actually flattened, and set production schedules to that curve instead of commissioning one hero film over eight weeks.

WARC's survey of 1,000 marketing executives found 43 percent think social advertising is getting less effective and 58 percent say their own buying practices make a platform hard to drop even when traffic falls, while social spend grows 21.3 percent to 394.6 billion dollars this year and 40 percent doubt short-form video builds a brand the way television does.  Stop spending on the platform you would least like to defend in a review, for four weeks, holding everything else steady, so you have a measured answer rather than a belief.

A DJ filmed himself setting his Rimowa suitcase on fire in the spring, and Away spent six months turning that complaint about a competitor into an October campaign timed to its own aluminium relaunch, with sales of that line up 20 percent year on year by the brand's own account.  Search your category for creators complaining about your competitors' products, then contact the one whose complaint lines up with something you are shipping in the next two quarters rather than the one with the most views.

Dior sold its holiday film on being entirely hand drawn, published behind-the-scenes footage of the animation, and then had the finished frames analysed one at a time, with the animator denying AI generation while confirming automated software produced some in-between frames.  Before publishing any making-of content, write down the single claim it proves and give the footage to somebody outside the production to try to disprove it, then change the claim rather than hiding the step.

The biggest measured live audience of the last fortnight was 1,119,734 people watching World of Warcraft on Twitch at once on 4 November, while the 14.47 million hours watched figure from the same launch covers two days and every channel streaming the game, and YouTube runs a 24-hour Grand Theft Auto stream with 31 creator channels next Thursday.  Put peak concurrents, average concurrents and total airtime into every live sponsorship contract you sign, and judge the audience on the average.

Fetch is running a six-part holiday series in which the sponsors' products are the receipts the heroine uses to find a man, one brand per episode, a new episode every three days, and viewers paid in app points for watching; its 96 percent completion figure comes from tests of a format that pays people to finish.  Give each episode of your next branded series a single sponsor whose product does a job in the plot, and get brand sign-off on the story outline rather than on a finished cut.

A 283,000 subscriber machining channel roughly doubled its median views, from 69,386 to 132,979, by starting a second build series alongside the first rather than extending it, and shows no paid sponsor in any of its last ten video descriptions.  Count how many videos on your own brand channel a brand-new viewer could start with, and if the answer is none, commission a part one.
